name: Monoculturalism
summary: Monoculturalism holds that a state should rest on one shared national culture, language and set of values, which newcomers and minorities are expected to adopt rather than preserve alongside it. Its adherents argue that cultural diversity and group identities erode trust, cohesion and national identity, and so favour assimilation, a common language and limits on immigration. In its harshest forms it treats the dominant group's culture as superior and excludes or suppresses minorities.
scope: The mainstream assimilationist and cultural-nationalist strand as argued in Western debates since the 1990s: Samuel Huntington's defence of an Anglo-Protestant core, Schlesinger's critique of multicultural education, the German Leitkultur debate (Merz), and Merkel- and Cameron-style rejections of multiculturalism. It excludes racial-supremacist and ethnic-purity regimes, which the Wikipedia article also counts as monoculturalism, and the global-homogenisation sense of the term.

keyFigures.name: Samuel P. Huntington
keyFigures.role: Political scientist who argued that multiculturalism and weak assimilation threaten America's Anglo-Protestant national identity.

keyFigures.name: Arthur M. Schlesinger Jr.
keyFigures.role: Historian whose The Disuniting of America criticised multiculturalism as a threat to national unity.

keyFigures.name: Friedrich Merz
keyFigures.role: German CDU politician who in 2000 demanded immigrants assimilate to a German Leitkultur and proposed an annual immigration cap.

sources.author: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
sources.usedFor: Scholarly statement of critics' positions on group rights, religious exemptions, national language and national identity.

universal-healthcare.rationale: The sources discuss culture and integration, not health policy; adherents span Conservative, Christian Democrat and American conservative parties that differ on it.

cut-welfare.rationale: The doctrine does not address welfare levels (its welfare concern is who qualifies, see welfare-for-citizens), and proponents differ.

state-harmful.rationale: Monoculturalism asks the state to uphold and transmit a common culture (Leitkultur tests, citizenship tests), so it rejects the view that the state is unnecessary.

decide-locally.rationale: Neutral: the doctrine wants one national culture, which pulls toward national standards, but nothing says decisions must be centralised.

rehabilitation.rationale: Penal policy is outside the doctrine and its proponents split on it.

traditional-family.rationale: Huntington's Anglo-Protestant core includes traditional values, but the family is not a central claim of the doctrine.

more-religion-public.rationale: Huntington treats Christianity as part of the core culture, but Tibi and Leitkultur frame the core as secular Enlightenment values, so adherents are split.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Defending a single shared national culture against dilution is the core of the doctrine; Huntington calls Anglo-Protestant culture the bedrock of American identity and the Wikipedia article defines monoculturalism as preserving one culture.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Merz proposed an annual cap of 200,000 on what German society could absorb and Scheffer spoke of exhausted absorptive capacity, though others in the camp only demand better integration.

nation-first.rationale: A doctrine centred on one national culture tends to prioritise national interests, but the sources address culture rather than foreign policy.

open-borders.rationale: A doctrine that worries that scale and speed of immigration prevent assimilation (Huntington, Scheffer) rejects open borders.

one-party-rule.rationale: Proponents argue within liberal democracies (Merkel, Cameron, Schlesinger), so a single guiding party is not part of their case.

democracy-best.rationale: Huntington, Schlesinger and Cameron argue for national unity within democratic states, and Cameron's defence of democracy and the rule of law is among the core values listed.

separate-church-state.rationale: Leitkultur defenders (Tibi) stress secularism while Huntington counts Christianity as part of the core culture, so adherents split.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Leitkultur and Cameron's muscular liberalism ground the national culture in secular law, democracy and rights, not scripture.

ethnic-nation.rationale: The Wikipedia article ties monoculturalism to one social or ethnic group's culture, but Huntington's mainstream version defines the core by culture and creed, not descent.

civilizational-union.rationale: Huntington's civilizational thinking points that way, but the doctrine concerns one state's culture, so adherents are split.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Leitkultur stresses shared obligations to national values, but proponents also insist on individual rights as core values, so they split.

restore-past-order.rationale: Defenders of the existing national culture sometimes invoke a lost cohesion (Huntington on older assimilation), but the doctrine is not essentially restorationist.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: The doctrine is nationalist-cultural and operates within liberal democracies; class dictatorship is incompatible with it. None of the cited sources takes up this question, so the answer is an inference.

harm-principle.rationale: Leitkultur and Cameron want the state to promote shared values actively (muscular liberalism), which strains a pure harm principle, but they also defend liberal rights.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Critics of multiculturalism such as Kukathas and Barry deny group rights, but the cultural-unity case also asks citizens to uphold a collective culture, so only a mild lean.

media-academia-power.rationale: Huntington and Schlesinger blame academic and elite promotion of multiculturalism for weakening national identity, which echoes this claim, though they do not say it is the main power.

national-rebirth.rationale: Huntington warns of decline in national identity, but the doctrine does not call for radical rebirth.

bound-labor.rationale: No proponent defends serfdom and it conflicts with the liberal-democratic framework of the mainstream strand. None of the cited sources takes up this question, so the answer is an inference.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Schlesinger and Huntington criticise relativist multiculturalists who treat Western heritage as merely another power-laden tradition.

universal-morality.rationale: Tibi grounds Leitkultur in universal Enlightenment values while Huntington stresses a particular culture, so adherents split.

national-self-determination.rationale: A doctrine of one national culture sits naturally with nations governing themselves, but the sources address culture, not a right of nations to statehood.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Tibi's Leitkultur draws on Enlightenment reason while Huntington counts Protestant Christianity as part of the core, so adherents split.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Proponents link national solidarity to a shared identity (Barry, Gitlin on cohesion), which supports reserving benefits, though this is not a central claim.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Inherited cultural institutions carry the national culture the doctrine exists to preserve, so sacrificing them for new creation is rejected.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Huntington-style conservatives may favour traditional roles, but Cameron's muscular liberalism defends women's rights, so adherents split.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: The mainstream strand defines belonging by culture and creed and offers assimilation, not racial classification; Merkel, Cameron and Huntington all work within equal citizenship.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Huntington blames weak assimilation for the problem, Merz demanded that immigrants adopt Germany's core cultural values, and Merkel urged integration into German culture.

national-mission.rationale: Huntington treats American creed as national identity but the doctrine concerns domestic culture, not spreading it abroad.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Huntington criticises elite indifference to national identity but does not call elites corrupt.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Eugenic policy is not part of the mainstream strand and is incompatible with the liberal-democratic framing of its proponents.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Leitkultur and citizenship tests ask the state to promote a common culture, which exceeds a minimal state.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Huntington stresses that assimilation includes intermarriage, so discouraging mixing runs against the mainstream account.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The mainstream strand grounds national belonging in a creed of equal rights and offers assimilation to all; the Wikipedia article notes the ethnocentric form that does not.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: Huntington frames the Anglo-Protestant settler culture as the founding bedrock of the US, not as a colonial project.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Leitkultur and the assimilationist case want one common set of national norms and law, without parallel legal communities.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Leitkultur defenders ground the national culture in secular liberal values including freedom of worship; Cameron lists freedom of worship among them.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Huntington values Christian heritage while Leitkultur defenders favour secular schooling, so adherents split.

population-transfer.rationale: The Wikipedia article lists suppression and exclusion as forms of monoculturalism, but the mainstream proponents propose assimilation and immigration limits rather than expulsion.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Huntington's clash-of-civilizations work stresses rivalry among peoples, but the doctrine does not state it as a driver of progress.

vanguard-party.rationale: A vanguard party of revolutionaries is incompatible with the doctrine and with its democratic proponents. None of the cited sources takes up this question, so the answer is an inference.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Huntington warns of two peoples, cultures and languages, and Putnam and Blainey are cited for the claim that diversity erodes trust and cohesion; this is the central premise of the doctrine.

party-commands-army.rationale: Alien to the liberal-democratic framing of mainstream proponents.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Lammert and Huntington root identity in a particular culture and nation, which weighs against pooling sovereignty, though Lammert reframes at the European level.

clerical-rule.rationale: Leitkultur and muscular liberalism root authority in secular democracy and law, so rule by religious scholars is rejected.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Huntington and Schlesinger fault academic and elite promotion of multiculturalism for ignoring national feeling, but do not make the general claim.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Within the scope's mainstream strand, Cliteur argues against cultural relativism and holds that liberal Western norms are better than some alternatives, and Huntington defends the Anglo-Protestant creed as the core to be preserved; both reject the claim that cultures are only different.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: Huntington values Protestant heritage but does not address school curricula.

minority-language-support.rationale: Huntington explicitly opposes bilingual education and dual-language programmes as threats to a single common language of the nation.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Critics of multiculturalism such as Barry reject special accommodations for religion, and Leitkultur requires one common set of norms.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Leitkultur defenders favour secular supremacy while Huntington defends Christianity's cultural role, so adherents split.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Alien to the liberal-democratic framing of its proponents. None of the cited sources takes up this question, so the answer is an inference.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Rule of law is among the values Leitkultur and Cameron's speech name as core.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: Marxist theory foreign to the doctrine.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Leitkultur defenders and Cameron list freedom of worship among core values.

women-must-cover.rationale: Cameron's muscular liberalism and Leitkultur stress women's rights and secular norms, and are directed against practices seen as incompatible with national values.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Critics of multiculturalism object that separate self-governing minority institutions and enclaves undermine a shared identity, and Huntington opposes separate enclaves.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Alien to the doctrine and its parliamentary proponents. None of the cited sources takes up this question, so the answer is an inference.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Huntington and Schlesinger criticise multicultural education for reducing Western heritage to crimes, and the doctrine wants school history built around the national tradition.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Cliteur and Huntington hold Western culture superior, but they do not argue for rule over other societies.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Huntington blames race-based group identities for weakening national identity, which points to opposing racial preferences, but he does not discuss admissions.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: Marxist theory foreign to the doctrine.

native-born-offices.rationale: Ethnic forms of monoculturalism might favour it but the civic assimilationist form does not, so adherents split.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: Defence of inherited national heritage against Western heritage being reduced to crimes (Schlesinger) points to keeping the monuments.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Huntington holds that American institutions derive from a particular Anglo-Protestant culture, and Cliteur treats Western institutions as culturally specific.

single-official-language.rationale: Huntington says immigrants can share the American dream only in English and opposes bilingual programmes, and critics cite language tests as policy.

religious-nation.rationale: Huntington stresses Protestant culture but defines identity by culture and creed, while Leitkultur defenders define it secularly, so adherents split.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: Marxist feminist claim foreign to the doctrine.

majority-settlement.rationale: Ethnic forms of monoculturalism could back it but mainstream proponents argue for assimilation, so adherents split.

holocaust-denial.rationale: Mainstream proponents appeal to liberal-democratic Western values; denial is outside the doctrine. None of the cited sources takes up this question, so the answer is an inference.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Cameron and Leitkultur defenders cite liberal values among the core; cultural conservatives might differ.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Proponents defend democracy and free speech as core values.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Leitkultur and Cameron's muscular liberalism list freedom of speech and worship as national values.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: Rejected by Leitkultur and muscular liberalism, which defend secular constitutional government.

alienated-labor.rationale: Marxist concept foreign to the doctrine.

islam-incompatible.rationale: Cliteur argues Western culture and law are superior to some non-Western practices and Merz and Scheffer targeted failed integration, but Tibi and Cameron separate Islam from extremism, so it is a lean only.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Leitkultur and muscular liberalism ground authority in secular democracy and law.

religious-dress-in-state.rationale: Quebec's Bill 21 and French-style laïcité fit single-culture views while Anglo-American proponents oppose such bans, so adherents split.

domination-women-nature.rationale: Ecofeminist claim foreign to the doctrine.

reification.rationale: Marxist concept foreign to the doctrine.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: Marxist critique foreign to the doctrine.

racial-franchise.rationale: The mainstream strand offers assimilation and citizenship on cultural terms, and Merkel, Cameron and Huntington all work within a universal franchise.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: Huntington treats intermarriage as a sign of assimilation, so restricting it opposes the mainstream strand.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Huntington counts Christianity as part of the national core and Leitkultur defenders favour secular neutrality, not state atheism.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Alien to the doctrine and its law-and-order centre-right proponents. None of the cited sources takes up this question, so the answer is an inference.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: Huntington opposes institutionalised communal division; consociational power-sharing between communities contradicts the single-culture ideal.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: The sources concern culture and integration, not poverty relief; adherents among conservatives lean to charity while Christian Democrats back the welfare state.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: The sources discuss a shared culture, not church governance; adherents run from Christian conservatives who oppose it to secular ones who accept it.

rent-control.rationale: Housing policy is outside the sources; adherents across conservative parties split on rent caps.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: Adherents are split between Atlanticist conservatives and sovereignty-minded nationalists; the sources are silent.

independent-unions.rationale: The sources discuss culture and integration, not labour; adherents differ.

socialism-needs-workers-power.rationale: Not a monocultural issue; adherents span left and right.

local-essentials-public.rationale: Not a monocultural issue; adherents differ on public ownership.

second-chamber.rationale: Not a monocultural issue; adherents differ on legislative design.

family-wage.rationale: Not a monocultural issue; adherents differ.

person-over-state.rationale: Adherents emphasise shared national values over individual preference, but the mainstream strand also upholds individual rights; split.

racial-group-interests.rationale: The mainstream strand in scope defends a shared national culture, not racial groups, and excludes racial-supremacist regimes.

racial-pride.rationale: The mainstream strand speaks of national culture, not race; adherents split.

language-defines-nation.rationale: Adherents stress a shared language as the core of a state's culture, but their nation is bounded by the state, so the statement's cross-border claim splits them.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: Adherents warn of internal fragmentation (s1) more than of foreign plots, and are split on external ones.

free-public-college.rationale: The ideology is about culture and assimilation and does not take a stand on tuition; adherents are split by general economic views.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Adherents work within existing parliamentary states and defend their institutions; revolutionary replacement of the state is far from the position.

sacred-nation.rationale: Huntington and the Leitkultur debate ground national identity in a shared culture and civic creed, but they argue in civic and cultural terms; none of them presents the nation as sacred.

farm-price-support.rationale: The sources cover culture and integration, not farm policy; adherents range across parties that differ on farm subsidies.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: The Leitkultur debate names secular core values such as equality as what newcomers must accept, which includes equal property rights for women. None of the cited sources takes up this question, so the answer is an inference.

immigrants-learn-language.rationale: Huntington argues English must be the common language and opposes bilingual education, and Merz's Leitkultur demands newcomers assimilate.

no-compulsory-union.rationale: The sources deal with culture and integration, not labour law, and adherents across conservative parties differ on union membership.

negative-income-tax.rationale: Welfare design is outside the monocultural case and its proponents differ across parties.

women-suffrage.rationale: Mainstream adherents accept women's equal political rights, and Leitkultur versions list sexual equality among the secular core values.

religion-oppresses-women.rationale: Leitkultur critics often cite Islam on women's status while Christian conservative adherents reject the claim, so adherents are split.

homestead-ownership.rationale: The sources concern culture and integration, not property; adherents from conservative parties differ on first-claim ownership.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Huntington's Anglo-Protestant core is cultural rather than doctrinal, and adherents are split on literal scripture.

national-church-status.rationale: Huntington's Protestant core and Cameron-style appeals to Christian heritage favour a place for the traditional church, though strands differ.

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: The sources oppose separate group rights and want minorities to join one national culture, which leans against minority autonomy, but they do not discuss territorial arrangements for regional minorities.

close-ties-china.rationale: Nothing in the monocultural case bears on China policy, and proponents differ.

self-ownership.rationale: The sources discuss culture and integration, not self-ownership; proponents span liberal and communitarian conservatives.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: Leitkultur proponents ground the shared culture in secular core values such as the constitution, though Huntington stresses Protestant heritage.

distribution-by-process.rationale: The sources discuss culture and integration, not distributive justice; adherents range from free-market to welfare-state conservatives.

racism-not-main-obstacle.rationale: Critics of multiculturalism usually attribute disadvantage to culture, language and integration rather than racism, but the sources do not take this position directly.

multipolar-world.rationale: Huntington argued for a world of civilizations, but other adherents favour a leading Western or national power; the sources do not settle it.

patriotism-serves-workers.rationale: Huntington and Merkel-style critics link national loyalty to social trust and cohesion, which the sources tie to a shared community; solidarity with workers abroad is not claimed.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: The doctrine does not address welfare levels (its welfare concern is who qualifies, see welfare-for-citizens), and proponents differ. (Carried over from cut-welfare, "Welfare programs create dependency and should be cut.", with the value reversed, 2026-11-11.)

missingStatements.text: Immigrants and their children should adopt the country's common language and way of life rather than keep separate communities.
missingStatements.rationale: Huntington and Merz both frame the problem as enclaves and failed assimilation and ask newcomers to take on the core culture.

missingStatements.text: Schools should not teach the history and values of minority cultures as separate subjects alongside the national culture.
missingStatements.rationale: Schlesinger and Huntington attack multicultural education and group-identity curricula as weakening common national identity.

missingStatements.text: Applicants for citizenship should have to pass a test of the national language, history and values.
missingStatements.rationale: Citizenship tests (Australia from 2007, German state tests) are the policy instruments the assimilationist critics of multiculturalism endorse.
missingStatements.declined: Citizenship tests are a narrow policy instrument; long-naturalization-wait and assimilate-immigrants cover the position.

notes: The doctrine is thin on economics, foreign policy and most social questions, so many answers are low-confidence inferences from the mainly centre-right politics of its proponents. A civic form (Huntington, Tibi, Cameron) and an ethnic form (as described in the Wikipedia article) differ on ethnic-nation, citizenship-by-descent and exclusion; the profile follows the civic form.
